chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Al-Hasan ibn ibn Mahboub, from Sadeer al-Sayrafi, who said:
Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said in a lengthy Hadith: When Allah resurrects the believer from his grave,

a resemblance (image) comes out with him, walking in front of him. Every time the believer sees a horror from the horrors of the Day of Resurrection, the resemblance says to him, 'Do not panic and do not grieve, and receive glad tidings of joy and honor from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.'
Until he stands before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, so He reckons him with an easy reckoning, and commands that he be taken to Paradise, and the resemblance is in front of him.

So the believer says to him, 'May Allah have mercy on you! What a good exit it was that you came out with me from my grave, and you have not ceased giving me glad tidings of joy and honor from Allah, until I saw that.'
And he says, 'Who are you?' So it says, 'I am the joy which you caused to enter upon your believer brother in the world. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, created me from it to give you glad tidings.'
ai.seo_question: What is the 'resemblance' that accompanies the believer after resurrection?
ai.summary: In Shia exegesis, this 'resemblance' (mithal) is understood as a tangible manifestation of the believer's inner spiritual state, specifically the joy he generated in others, which accompanies him as a witness to his social piety. This concept highlights the metaphysical reality of 'cause and effect' in the afterlife, where good deeds take on a personified form to intercede for their owner, reinforcing the significance of spreading happiness (surur) as a distinct act of worship. The narrative underscores the transition from the fear of the grave to the ease of reckoning, illustrating how divine mercy is often mediated through the very virtues the believer cultivated.
